claims.text: The identity of X in CrFeCoNiX governs the formation and persistence of a coherent protective oxide scale above 900 °C.
Si additions to CrFeCoNi promote dense, slow-growing, adherent SiO2-containing scales.
Al additions to CrFeCoNi promote dense, slow-growing, adherent Al2O3-containing scales.
The beneficial effects of Si and Al arise from high oxide-formation enthalpies and low diffusivities.
Mn in CrFeCoNiMn is preferentially oxidized and produces non-protective oxides.
Mn-containing CrFeCoNi alloys undergo rapid oxidation and form less coherent, cracked, and spall-prone scales.
The poor scale behavior associated with Mn is caused by higher cation diffusivity and lower thermodynamic stability.
Mn has a propensity to form volatile oxide phases under the stated exposure conditions.
Si- and Al-containing scales have low interfacial lattice misfit, whereas Mn-containing scales have greater lattice mismatch and residual stress.
Element X changes oxidation kinetics and scale stability by altering selective oxidation at the metal/oxide interface.
Slow oxide growth and low interfacial strain allow Si- and Al-containing scales to remain adherent during thermal cycling.
Mn oxidation depletes Mn from the alloy immediately beneath the oxide layer.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiAl will maintain stable coherent scales during prolonged cyclic exposure above 900 °C.
CrFeCoNiMn will develop unstable oxide layers that crack or spall during prolonged cyclic exposure above 900 °C.
The CrFeCoNi baseline will show oxidation behavior intermediate between the Si/Al-containing alloys and the Mn-containing alloy.
Identical gas atomization and rapid-solidification processing will minimize extraneous microstructural differences among the compared alloys.
The proposed comparison is restricted to controlled, nominally single-phase solid-solution alloys exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres under cyclic thermal conditions.
Minor processing-induced microstructural variations could alter quantitative diffusion rates and oxidation kinetics.
Comparable scale coherence, interfacial strain, and long-term stability in Mn- and Si/Al-containing alloys would falsify the proposed element-specific mechanism.
